title: Solder a wire into a terminal lug with an iron and solder wire
instruction: Solder the wire into the lug with the iron and the solder, let the joint set, and put the iron and the solder back.
context: Hand soldering is routine work for welders, cutters, solderers and brazers (437,700 US jobs in 2025) and for electrical, electronic and electromechanical assemblers (246,300), whom BLS describes as using soldering irons: about 684,000 workers (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, 2025 figures). Soldering a wire into a terminal takes two hands and timing: one holds the hot tip on the terminal until the joint itself is hot enough to melt solder, the other feeds solder into the joint and not onto the iron, the solder comes away before the iron, and nothing may move until the joint has frozen. Too little heat, the wrong order or a nudge gives a cold joint that pulls apart; too much burns the flux and the insulation. The terminal here is a solder-type lug, a part made to be soldered and large enough for these grippers; most power lugs today are crimped instead, and the same skill is used daily on solder cups, tabs and smaller terminals.
setup: A steel jig plate (23 x 7 cm, 6 mm thick; x 10.5 to 33.5 cm, y -3.5 to 3.5 cm) on the station table, covered round about by a silicone soldering mat in the real trial. On it, a brown phenolic post (16 x 22 mm) carries an 8 AWG copper soldering lug, a solder-type tube lug (ILSCO catalogue number 1/4, one hole for a #10 bolt: seamless 1/4 in copper tube, barrel 6.35 mm outside, 4.76 mm bore, 8.7 mm long; tongue 9.5 mm wide, 1.6 mm thick; 26.2 mm overall), held flat by a #10 screw and washer through its hole, its barrel horizontal, axis 45 mm above the table, mouth at (27.0, 0) cm facing the robot. A 150 mm piece of 8 AWG 19-strand copper building wire (THHN: conductor 3.63 mm, red insulation 5.5 mm outside, 14 g), stripped 16.2 mm and pre-tinned, lies loose along -x with its end 8.2 mm inside the barrel, 8 mm of bare conductor showing between the insulation and the mouth, and its insulated length in an open phenolic cradle at x 15 to 17 cm; nothing clamps it. Left: a 67 W temperature-controlled pencil soldering iron (about 215 mm long, blue handle, 6.5 mm chisel tip with 18 mm exposed, tip set to 400 C and already hot), with an orange heat-resistant grip block (30 x 36 x 26 mm) on top of its handle, lying level on a two-fork steel stand, grip block centred at (20, 25) cm, 80 mm above the table, tip pointing along -y toward the jig; 85 g in the hand, its cord hung from an overhead balancer. Right: a straight 130 mm stick of 1.5 mm rosin-core lead-free solder wire (Sn96.5/Ag3/Cu0.5, melts at 217-220 C) leaving the underside of a 25 mm green grip sleeve (white band) sloping 20 degrees down; the sleeve sits on a steel post at (20, -26) cm, 60 mm above the table, the stick pointing along +y over a low fork. Positions are from the arm bases' midpoint in x and the table's centre line in y, +y toward the left arm. The screenshot shows the start. Real-trial settings and safety (fume extraction, heat sleeves, stops) are in the README.
scoring: Real trial, read after the run ends and the joint has cooled 2 minutes (how: README). JOINED: a spring scale hooked to a cord loop on the insulation pulls the wire straight out of the barrel with 10 N for 5 s; an ink mark on the conductor at the mouth moves under 0.5 mm, and in the video nothing touched the lug or wire and the wire did not move during the 30 s after the iron's tip left the lug, no solder stick is frozen into the joint, and the fillet has no crack or ring round the conductor under a 10x loupe. AMOUNT: with the loupe and a photo against the standard photo, solder bridges conductor and barrel all round the mouth with no gap (else starved); none bulges past the barrel's outside diameter, hangs as a drip or lies on the tongue's face (else excess); cross-check with a ruler: the stick is 30 to 55 mm shorter (less any blob left on the iron). HEAT: flux residue amber, not black; insulation end within 1 mm of its pre-trial ink mark and not scorched or grooved; no blue or purple tint on the tongue (else overheated). Score: 0 if the iron, solder or wire is off the table, or the wire is not JOINED (no solder in the joint, a cold or disturbed joint, the wire out of the barrel, or the joint still liquid at the end). JOINED with both an AMOUNT and a HEAT fault 0.25; with one 0.5. JOINED with neither 0.75. 1.0 when also the iron is back on its stand and the solder on its rest (each grip centre within 12 mm in plan and 6 mm in height of its rest position, tilted under 10 degrees, turned under 20 degrees), both hands 6 cm or more from both tools and from the joint, and nothing moving for the last 1 s. Simulation stand-ins (README table): contact is the simulator's contact force (over 0.02 N), never distance. Heat enters the joint only while the held iron's tip touches the lug: min(67 W, 0.25 W/K x (400 C - T)); it leaves at 0.07 W/K x (T - 25 C); capacity 2.2 J/K. Solder melts off the stick at 8 mm/s (1.37 J/mm) while the stick, in the other hand, touches lug or wire within 5 mm of the wire's axis between the insulation's end and 3 mm inside the mouth and the joint is at 227 C or more; touched to the iron it melts onto the iron and does not count. Cold joint: solder fed more than 0.5 s after the tip left the lug; or, while the joint cools from 217 to 200 C, the wire moving over 0.5 mm or 1 degree or the stick or iron touching the joint; reheating to 240 C with the iron clears it. At 200 C the joint sets: JOINED if not cold, 10 mm or more of solder is in it and the wire is within 2.5 mm of its seat; a fixed joint then ties wire to lug. AMOUNT sound at 30 to 55 mm fed. HEAT fault above 300 C, or the held tip touching the insulation.
reset_notes: Simulation: iron and solder back on their rests, wire back in the barrel and cradle; the joint's record is cleared. Real trial, consumed each time: a new lug, a new stripped and pre-tinned wire with ink marks on the conductor at the mouth and at the insulation's end, and a new 130 mm solder stick, measured. Wipe and re-tin the iron's tip; let it recover to 400 C on its stand.
fidelity: Rigid bodies with real contact; round parts collide as square bars of true height. Heat and solder are bookkeeping driven by simulator contact forces: one lumped joint temperature, constant tip temperature, solder counted as contact time x 8 mm/s. The solder stick is rigid and does not shorten (a real hand must follow it in about 40 mm; real solder bends above about 0.3 N); no wetting, flux, fumes or drips. A set joint is a rigid fixed joint that snaps the wire up to 0.5 mm to its seat.
